name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,323

clue.text: Note about touring the same lake

indicators.note: to tour something is to go all the way round it, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
ca is short for circa, Latin for about
a second copy of the note-plus-about pair just built

explanation.surface: A musician hums the same note while sailing round a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The same' asks for a repeat of the note-plus-about pair already built, and 'touring' puts the first copy around the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Titicaca is the large lake straddling the border of Peru and Bolivia, an example of the class.

clue.text: Shows off very close relatives

blocks.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very
aunts are near kin

explanation.surface: Someone boasts about how tight their family bonds are.
explanation.definitionFit: To vaunt is to boast or brag, so the verb is a synonym for showing off.

clue.text: Vicar let slip what this answer is?

indicators.note: a slip is a mistake, and letters let slip come out muddled and out of order

blocks.note: the two words supply eight letters

explanation.surface: A clergyman blurts out a secret, prompting the question of what it was.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points at the grid itself: this entry is a down light, so it runs vertically.
explanation.definitionFit: Down entries in a crossword run from top to bottom, so the solution's own orientation is upright.

clue.text: Maybe we spur on Napoleon when struggling to cross river

indicators.note: things struggling are thrashing about, so the letters are thrown into disorder
to cross something here is to straddle it, so the mixed letters sit either side of one letter

blocks.note: fourteen letters to rearrange
R is the usual abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Troops urge the Emperor onward as he battles to get his army across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks the definition as an example: we is one such word.
explanation.definitionFit: We is a first-person plural pronoun, one instance of a word standing in for people by grammatical person.

clue.text: Food is served up with artificial stuffing

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means brought upwards, so the word reads from bottom to top
stuffing is put inside something, so one piece goes into the middle of another

blocks.note: taken as written
camp means affected or deliberately exaggerated

explanation.surface: A dish arrives filled with some processed, fake stuffing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served up' fits the food surface, but in a down light it means the word is read from the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi are breaded langoustines, a dish familiar in British pubs, so they are an example of food.

clue.text: Coherent member must have done it

blocks.note: first meaning: logically connected
second meaning: anyone who is a member must once have enlisted or signed on

explanation.surface: A sensible club member is accused of a misdeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Done it' sounds like a whodunnit accusation, but it means the act of enrolling that every member has performed.
explanation.definitionFit: Joined-up describes connected, integrated thinking, and as a verb phrase it means enlisted in an organisation.

clue.text: Relaxed companion, male not female

indicators.note: putting one thing and not another means the first takes the place of the second

blocks.note: a fellow is a companion or comrade
M is the abbreviation for male
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A laid-back friend turns out to be a man rather than a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The F at the front of FELLOW is swapped for M.
explanation.definitionFit: Mellow describes someone easygoing and calm, a synonym for relaxed.

clue.text: Illusion of motorway madness?

blocks.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI in crosswords
rage is fury or madness

explanation.surface: Road rage on a motorway is likened to a hallucination.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds; the digit 1 doubles as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion, such as water seemingly shimmering on a hot road.

clue.text: Held tightly when death consumes

indicators.note: what consumes something swallows it whole, so one piece ends up inside the other

blocks.note: death is one's end
close means tightly, as in held close

explanation.surface: Someone is clutched tightly as death overtakes them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held tightly' looks like one definition, but tightly belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Something enclosed is held in or shut in on all sides, a synonym for contained or held.

clue.text: Book about pub causes a sensational complaint

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece is placed around the other

blocks.note: Titus is an epistle in the New Testament
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A book about pubs causes an outraged complaint from readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sensational' suggests scandal, but here it means relating to the senses: the ailment is a hearing one.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinnitus is a ringing in the ears, a disorder of the sense of hearing, so an ailment of sensation.

clue.text: Squeeze fish on back of aquarium

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept
placed on means coming after, so this piece is attached to the end of the other

blocks.note: the final letter of aquarium
to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: Someone presses a fish against the rear glass of a tank.
explanation.definitionFit: A mangle is a wringer with rollers, and to mangle laundry is to squeeze water out of it; as a verb it also means to crush.

clue.text: A long way from bobby arresting bum

indicators.note: a policeman arresting someone holds them, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: a bobby is a British police officer, a PC or police constable
arse is British slang for the backside

explanation.surface: A long chase ends with a constable nabbing a tramp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as a vagrant being arrested, but it is the British slang for the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsec is an astronomical unit of distance, about 3.26 light years, which is certainly a great distance.

clue.text: Following fix, somehow United ultimately have to make final

indicators.note: the following piece comes after, so the second part is placed behind the first
somehow suggests some unknown arrangement, so the letters may be shuffled
ultimately means at the very end, so only the last letter is kept

blocks.note: to nail something is to fix it in place
the last letter of United
to own is to have

explanation.surface: A football commentator says United must somehow seal their place in the final.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal covers the last letter of United and the word for have; their mix happens to land in the order written.
explanation.definitionFit: To nail down an agreement is to settle it firmly and make it definite.

clue.text: Match round tube with nameless objects to make solid figures

indicators.note: without a name means the abbreviation for name is taken out
round means surrounding, so one piece is wrapped about the other

blocks.note: to parallel something is to match it
ends are aims or objects
a pipe is a tube

explanation.surface: Someone builds geometric shapes by fitting a tube against various items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nameless' strips N, the abbreviation for name, from the word for objects before it goes round the tube.
explanation.definitionFit: A parallelepiped is a three-dimensional shape with six parallelogram faces, a type of solid in geometry.

clue.text: OK with "I is into reggae 'n' rum"

indicators.note: rum means odd or peculiar, so the letters are put into a strange order
a letter that is into something has been placed inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to loving Caribbean music and rum, and others are fine with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink from the reggae scene, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Being OK with a proposal means consenting to it, so the participle is a synonym for content with it.

clue.text: Undemanding dad getting out more?

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
each word replaced by its opposite: out becomes in, more becomes less

explanation.surface: A father wonders whether going out more would make life easier.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the trick: the wordplay asks for the opposites of out and more.
explanation.definitionFit: Something painless causes no trouble or effort, so it is easy and makes few demands.

clue.text: Philosopher, old and extremely gentle, eats out

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only first and last letters are kept
someone who eats out takes the meal in, so the diner surrounds what is eaten

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
the first and last letters of gentle
to dine out is to eat at a restaurant

explanation.surface: An aged, mild-mannered thinker goes out for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eats out' does double duty: it gives DINES and says the other letters are taken in, giving DI(OGE)NES.
explanation.definitionFit: Diogenes of Sinope was the Greek Cynic philosopher who famously lived in a large jar.

clue.text: I receive alternate parts of Team GB's fast car

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, a person who embraces; the clue speaks in that person's own voice

indicators.note: alternate parts means every other letter, so only the second, fourth and sixth are kept

blocks.note: every second letter of Team GB
a racer is a fast car

explanation.surface: A British Olympic athlete's sports car is welcomed by the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks as the answer itself: one who embraces could say 'I receive' of a guest.
explanation.definitionFit: An embracer is one who welcomes or takes in, so the speaker accepting something is that person.

clue.text: Poor setter has for the most part to get on

indicators.note: for the most part means not all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as me
people who get on agree

explanation.surface: A struggling crossword setter mostly manages to get along with others.
explanation.walkthrough: AGREE loses its last E to give AGRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Meagre means scanty or deficient in quantity, so a meagre portion is a poor one.

clue.text: Risk transfer, clubs providing substitute for good

indicators.note: providing a substitute for one thing puts something else in its place

blocks.note: to transfer is to change trains or buses
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A football club gambles on a transfer to sign a replacement player.
explanation.walkthrough: The G in CHANGE is replaced by C.
explanation.definitionFit: To chance something is to take a gamble with it, so the word is a synonym for hazard.

clue.text: Contemptible person, no saint, that may assist writer

indicators.note: no means without, so the abbreviation that follows is removed

blocks.note: a stinkpot is a nasty, despicable person
ST is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A nasty, unholy character offers to help an author.
explanation.walkthrough: STINKPOT loses its ST.
explanation.definitionFit: An inkpot holds ink for a pen and so serves someone writing by hand.

clue.text: Light reading facilitated by this?

blocks.note: first meaning: to set alight
second meaning: the brand of e-reader used for digital books

explanation.walkthrough: 'Light reading' sounds like a pleasant paperback, but the first word is a verb meaning set fire to.
explanation.definitionFit: To kindle is to ignite a fire, and Amazon's Kindle is a widely used electronic book reader.

clue.text: Former labour leader from country area

blocks.note: Wales is a country of the UK
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: An ex-leader of the Labour Party hails from a rural part of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: Lower-case 'labour' hides that this is not the British Labour Party but a trade union leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Lech Walesa led Poland's Solidarity trade union, a workers' movement, before becoming president.

clue.text: Number one yearning? Not now

blocks.note: No. is the abbreviation for number
one who longs is a longer

explanation.surface: The top-ranked dreamer insists that the moment is not right.
explanation.definitionFit: No longer means formerly but not at present, so it signals something that has ceased.

clue.text: Fine wine as well as cold game served by a king

indicators.note: served by something means preceded by it, so that piece is placed first

blocks.note: GR, Georgius Rex, is the cipher of King George
and means as well as
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: A king is served a fine wine along with chilled game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' suggests venison on the menu, but it is rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand cru is the top classification of French vineyards, used for the best wines.

clue.text: Tommy blowing one fuse

indicators.note: blowing something means losing or wasting it, so a letter is lost

blocks.note: Tommy is slang for a British private soldier
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A British soldier blows a fuse in a fit of temper.
explanation.walkthrough: SOLDIER loses its I.
explanation.definitionFit: Solder is a metal alloy melted to join wires, so to solder is to fuse metal parts.
